video_title: Austan Goolsbee Is Worried the Economy Is Overheating
gist: Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, interviewed at Jackson Hole in August 2026 ahead of Chair Kevin Warsh's speech, says his reaction function is now heavily tilted toward inflation risk: services inflation that can't be blamed on tariffs or oil is his tripwire, and he dissented against front-loading rate cuts. He argues AI data-center capex is not yet economy-wide overheating but would make policy 'not restrictive enough' if it spills out of its lane, and he backs less forward guidance while defending reaction-function communication as a distinct and valuable thing.

themes.theme: Policy stance and Goolsbee's inflation reaction function

insights.claim: Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee refuses to label current policy restrictive or not, arguing the answer depends entirely on the underlying inflation rate: if inflation is running 3%-plus, the real policy rate is far lower than it looks versus a world where inflation is heading back to target.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: Anyone modeling the Fed's next move should track the underlying/services inflation run-rate rather than the nominal funds rate versus estimates of neutral, because that is the variable this policymaker says determines the stance.
insights.quote: Depends what you think the underlying inflation rate is.

insights.claim: Goolsbee's stated long-run landing spot for US monetary policy is roughly a 3% nominal policy rate, 2% inflation and a 1% real rate.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: A concrete anchor for terminal-rate pricing from a sitting Fed president; front-end curve pricing far above or below a 3% terminal implies disagreement with a centrist FOMC voice.
insights.quote: I loosely think 3% rates with 2% inflation and 1% real is kind of Eventual landing spot.

insights.claim: Goolsbee says his reaction function is heavily geared toward getting evidence that the current inflation shock is not persistent, and that services inflation — which cannot be blamed on tariffs or oil — is the component that would make him nervous.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: Core services ex-goods is the print that flips this Fed president hawkish; goods/tariff-driven upside surprises are far less likely to move his vote.

insights.claim: Goolsbee dissented at the final meeting of last year against cutting rates, objecting to front-loading cuts on the assumption that inflation would prove transitory, and noting the government was shut down so the committee did not even have the data.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: Documents a named hawkish dissent and the specific condition — evidence inflation is returning to 2% — that would be needed to bring him back onside for further easing.
insights.quote: I'm not comfortable front loading the rate cuts, counting on this inflation to be transitory and go away.

insights.claim: Goolsbee describes the inflation path as substantial progress that then stalled out, then started going the wrong way, with only a modest recent easing that he still calls iffy — and says the last six months of inflation data have not been looking great.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: A sitting Fed president characterizing the disinflation as stalled and reversing argues against pricing a smooth cutting cycle and raises the tail risk of a hold-or-hike pivot.

themes.theme: AI data-center capex vs. aggregate overheating

insights.claim: Goolsbee draws a sharp line between sectoral crowding-out from AI data centers and genuine economy-wide overheating: bidding away electricians and construction crews from other industries is not overheating unless it escapes its lane and pushes up wages and prices in the broader economy.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: A usable test for whether AI capex becomes a monetary-policy problem: watch aggregate wage and price measures and national unemployment/GDP, not anecdotes about contractor shortages.
insights.quote: It has to get out of its lane of just direct competition and drive up wages, drive up prices outside of just its lane.

insights.claim: Goolsbee says that if high investment and high growth start pushing aggregate inflation the wrong way, then by definition policy is not restrictive enough — an explicitly hawkish contingency tied to the AI capex boom.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: Gives a channel by which an AI capex boom translates into rate hikes rather than cuts; a hawkish repricing risk that equity investors treating AI spend as pure growth may be underweighting.
insights.quote: And if inflation starts going the wrong way, driven by just old fashion, investment is so high and growth is so high that that we're getting that impulse, that then I think it's not restrictive enough.

insights.claim: In the Chicago Fed's district, business contacts in Cedar Rapids, Iowa report that data centers are buying up all the land, driving up prices, blocking other construction and making HVAC technicians unobtainable.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: Ground-level confirmation that hyperscaler buildouts are consuming Midwest land and skilled trades — bullish for regional land, electrical and HVAC contractors, and a cost headwind for competing non-AI construction.
insights.quote: the data centers are buying up all the land. They're driving up the prices nobody can construct can do any construction. You can't get you can't get an Hvac person.

insights.claim: Goolsbee pushes back on the volume of executive complaints about AI-driven cost pressure, saying he hears about it 'maybe too much' and noting that people have always complained about not being able to get contractors and now simply blame data centers.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: Suggests survey and anecdotal evidence of AI cost pressure is inflated by attribution bias; don't over-extrapolate earnings-call complaints into a macro inflation call.
insights.quote: you hear it from business executives, but in some ways, I feel like maybe too much

insights.claim: Goolsbee dismisses r-star as an operational guide, calling it 'our Sasquatch' — a concept that exists but is never observable in real time and therefore useless for deciding the next policy move.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: Signals that arguments about policy stance framed around neutral-rate estimates will not move this policymaker; realized inflation and activity data will.
insights.quote: I always called our star our Sasquatch.

insights.claim: Goolsbee's key framework is that whether an AI productivity boom is inflationary depends on whether it is expected or unexpected: an unexpected productivity gain pushes inflation down and permits lower rates, while a widely hyped and anticipated future bounty causes people to spend ahead of it, overheats the economy in the short run and forces rate hikes — the mid-to-late 1990s pattern.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: The single most tradeable idea in the conversation: the louder the AI-boom narrative, the more likely the Fed hikes into it, inverting the usual 'tech productivity means lower rates' assumption.
insights.quote: the bigger the hype, the more we're about to have a giant bounty that's going to come from technology. You can easily overheat the economy in the short run and you have to raise the rates.

insights.claim: Goolsbee cautions that measured productivity growth has been crummy for six months in a row, so nobody should conclude an AI-driven change of era has actually manifested in the data.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: The hard data does not yet support the AI-productivity-miracle case; a hawkish combination of high AI capex plus weak measured productivity is exactly the overheating setup he fears.
insights.quote: we've now got in six months in a row of pretty crummy productivity growth

themes.theme: Serial supply shocks and the transitory debate

insights.claim: Goolsbee warned before Liberation Day tariffs that the Covid lesson is that a large enough supply shock, even one that is theoretically a one-off price-level move, can take far longer to fade than initially forecast — and stacking an oil price shock on top of tariffs before the first one cleared makes that far dicier.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: The mechanism by which the Fed's 'look through tariffs' stance breaks down; overlapping supply shocks are the path to a genuine hiking scare.
insights.quote: if a supply shock, that is that supposed to be transitory? If it's big enough, can end up taking a lot longer than than we initially forecast

insights.claim: Goolsbee attributes the abnormal low-hiring, low-firing labor market to compounded uncertainty from tariffs and war rather than to normal cyclical demand dynamics, and says this combination has no automatic policy playbook.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: Explains why payroll and claims data are giving muted signals and why a labor-market crack, if it comes, could arrive abruptly rather than through gradual deterioration.
insights.quote: that's what's led in the labor market to this kind of high, low hiring, low firing

insights.claim: Goolsbee attributes the post-Covid inflation episode roughly two-thirds to supply and one-third to demand, and calls out both sides of the debate for wanting it both ways — blaming stimulus for the run-up while crediting supply-chain healing for the decline.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: A quantified decomposition from a sitting policymaker; if supply dominates, the Fed's tolerance for looking through the next supply shock is greater than a purely demand-driven reading would imply.
insights.quote: I think it was loosely two thirds supply and one third demand

insights.claim: Goolsbee cites TIPS-implied inflation compensation holding steady around 2.3% CPI — which he says corresponds to the 2.0% PCE target — even while headline CPI approached 10%, as proof that the numerical inflation target worked as an anchor.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: Establishes the specific market variable the Fed watches for regime break: if TIPS breakevens drift materially above ~2.3% CPI, the anchor argument fails and the policy response would be far more aggressive.

insights.claim: Goolsbee argues that high wage growth does not prevent disinflation because wages are stickier than prices — shocks push prices up first and wages follow, so the sequence reverses on the way down too.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: Tells investors not to treat hot average hourly earnings prints as a blocker to Fed cuts; this policymaker explicitly discounts the wage-price-spiral read.
insights.quote: They're forgetting that wages are stickier than prices.

themes.theme: Bond market signals and policy reflexivity

insights.claim: Goolsbee explicitly discounts the view that rising long yields reflect a freak-out over US creditworthiness, pointing out that a roughly 5% to 5.25% long rate is historically pretty normal and inconsistent with genuine default pricing; he attributes the move to some mix of inflation expectations, a higher expected Fed path, and heavier issuance supply.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: The Fed is not treating long-end weakness as a fiscal-credibility event, so bets on a Fed intervention or yield-curve response to a 'debt scare' narrative lack official support.
insights.quote: I don't put that much credence on the argument that there's a general freak out about the credit worthiness of the United States

insights.claim: Goolsbee invokes Paul Volcker's rule that the Fed acts and the market reacts, warning about the reflection problem in which bond market moves partly just encode expectations of the Fed itself.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: Guards against circular trades that read market pricing as independent information about the Fed's next move; the Fed will not be led by the curve.
insights.quote: our job is to act. And the market's job is to react. And let's not get the order mixed up.

insights.claim: Responding to Kevin Warsh's argument that markets should play more ball and less referee, Goolsbee draws a distinction he supports — the Federal Reserve Act names maximum employment and stable prices and says nothing about stock or bond markets, so gathering information from markets is fine but taking direction from them is not.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: Flags a live philosophical split inside the FOMC over how much market signal should drive policy — a source of dissent risk and communication volatility under the new chair.
insights.quote: doesn't say anything about stock market, doesn't say anything about bond markets

themes.theme: Fed communications overhaul under Chair Warsh

insights.claim: Goolsbee personally endorses reducing forward guidance in the narrow sense of pre-committing to specific future rate moves, arguing it adds volatility and ties the committee's hands, while insisting that communicating a reaction function is a distinct and valuable practice that should continue.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: Expect the Fed to stop pre-announcing rate paths while still describing what data it is watching — meaning more meeting-to-meeting front-end volatility but not less information about the framework.
insights.quote: I think that's adds to volatility and threatens to get us into a tying of our hands that I don't think it's healthy.

insights.claim: Goolsbee identifies a specific structural flaw in the dot plot: the median rate dot and the median inflation forecast are not necessarily from the same person, so the SEP cannot actually be read as a reaction function even though that is what markets try to use it for.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: A technical reason to stop trading the SEP medians as a coherent policy rule, and a hint at what a redesigned dot plot might try to fix.
insights.quote: it doesn't actually serve as a reaction function

insights.claim: Goolsbee says he has been on public record for years opposing the Summary of Economic Projections because published forecasts that don't come true cost the Fed credibility, and notes an outside-led task force is currently reviewing Fed communications with press conferences, the dot plot and even the number of meetings all potentially on the table.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: Concrete probability that the SEP, dot plot or press-conference cadence gets scrapped or redesigned — a structural change in the information flow that rates desks and Fed-funds futures pricing depend on.
insights.quote: people can go back and look and say, wait, aren't you the bozos who said that?

insights.claim: Goolsbee says the FOMC feels very different under the new chair, who has a different worldview and has publicly said he wants to stir up more debate, and notes the unusual situation that the former chair has simply moved his seat over a couple of spaces and is still at the table.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: Points to a less consensus-driven committee and a higher dissent rate ahead, which raises the noise in Fed communications and the odds of surprise votes.

insights.claim: Goolsbee confirms that 'silent dissents' at the Fed are real only in the sense that non-voting regional presidents who disagree have no vote to cast and can express it solely through public speeches, and he rejects the sell-side implication that voting members cast votes against their own views.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: Read non-voter speeches rather than vote tallies to gauge true committee sentiment, and discount analyst attempts to count hidden dissent among actual voters.

insights.claim: Ahead of Chair Warsh's Jackson Hole speech, Goolsbee says what he will be watching for is the chair's broadly defined reaction function and specifically his read on whether inflation is transitory or persistent, because persistence would force action by the Fed.
insights.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
insights.so_what: Names the exact signal to parse from the new chair's first Jackson Hole address; a persistence framing would be a hawkish repricing catalyst for the front end.
insights.quote: I'm hyper focused on this question of is inflation going to be transitory or is it going to be persistent.
